clue.text: Male paid by performance, not at first unaccompanied

parts.note: a gig is a musical performance

indicators.note: says the opening letter of the word for unaccompanied is dropped

parts.note: a solo is played unaccompanied

explanation.surface: A man is paid according to how he performs, but at first he worked alone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not at first' removes the S of SOLO, leaving OLO.
explanation.definitionFit: A man paid to be a woman's companion or lover is the classic sense of this word.

clue.text: Keen exhibitionist just starting run — under arrest potentially right away?

definitions.text: Keen exhibitionist just starting run — under arrest potentially right away?

indicators.note: in a down clue the later pieces sit under the rearranged letters
what arrest could potentially become, its letters reworked into another order
tells us one R, the abbreviation for right, is taken out of arrest
only the opening letters of the two words are used

parts.note: R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: An eager show-off makes a dash and may soon be arrested — and off he goes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'right away' takes an R out of ARREST; 'potentially' rearranges the rest (ARRST less one R, i.e. AREST) as STREA. Under it go KE (starts of Keen exhibitionist) and R.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue describes a naked runner at a public event, a show-off who may well be arrested.

clue.text: Reticent about two newspapers appearing evasive

indicators.note: the word for reticent goes about, around, the newspapers

parts.note: a shy person is reticent
the i and the Financial Times (FT) are two British newspapers

explanation.surface: A quiet person, buried in a couple of papers, seems to be dodging something.
explanation.walkthrough: The i is a British national daily paper; FT is the Financial Times.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone shifty looks untrustworthy and avoids straight answers, a synonym for dodgy.

clue.text: See 8
Desert shade

definitions.meaning: to abandon someone, as on an island

explanation.surface: A colour found in the desert.
explanation.definitionFit: To strand someone is to abandon them; the same word names a dark red-brown colour.

clue.text: Supply kit, not primarily for a team of 3 15 15s?

indicators.note: read as 'supplely', i.e. flexibly, so the letters bend into a new order
the first letter of 'for' is not used

explanation.surface: An instruction to provide equipment, but not chiefly for a three-person team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' is not about providing: it is the adverb of supple, rearranging KIT and OR (for less F). 15 15s are GEE GEES, horses, with a nod to the Bee Gees, the three-brother theme.
explanation.definitionFit: A Russian carriage is drawn by three horses abreast; the word also means that team or any trio.

clue.text: Hat priced badly, going for a song

indicators.note: something done badly is messed up, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A poorly priced hat is going very cheap.
explanation.definitionFit: Something going for a song is sold for very little money, the idiom for very cheap.

clue.text: Singer Rod, extremely raunchy male (article by 1 down)

parts.note: a bar is a rod

indicators.note: only the extreme letters of raunchy are taken

parts.note: an is the indefinite article
I is the Roman numeral one
low means down, as in spirits

explanation.surface: A singer named Rod, a very racy man, writes a piece about a performance.
explanation.walkthrough: '1 down' looks like a cross-reference to 1 Down but is simply I (Roman one) and LOW (down). Barry Manilow is a US singer; Barry is also the eldest Bee Gee.
explanation.definitionFit: He is an American pop vocalist famous for ballads like Mandy and Copacabana.

clue.text: Succeed the first time? Don't be ridiculous!

parts.note: a plan that comes off succeeds
I is the Roman numeral for first, as in a monarch's title

explanation.surface: Getting it right at the first attempt? Surely not!
explanation.walkthrough: 'the first' is I as in Elizabeth I.
explanation.definitionFit: This exclamation is an idiom telling someone to stop talking nonsense.

clue.text: Things assumed to be true by singer, actor and model

parts.note: a robin is a songbird
givens are facts taken for granted

explanation.surface: A set of premises attributed to a singer, an actor and a model.
explanation.walkthrough: 'singer' looks like part of the list of people, but it is the bird. Robin is also a Bee Gee.
explanation.definitionFit: Robin Givens is an American actress and model, once married to Mike Tyson.

clue.text: See 18
See 25
Working with 10, new 14 15 pens article for the net

parts.note: a machine that is on is working
the number 10 is drawn as the letters I and O

indicators.note: to pen is to enclose, so the article sits inside the two letters

parts.note: the answers to 14 and 15 are the letter names for B and G
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A cryptic list of numbered items producing an article for netting.
explanation.walkthrough: '14 15' are BEE and GEE, letters B and G, which pen A. 10 is read as the shapes I and O.
explanation.definitionFit: In British football slang the goal net is called by this name, after the mesh sacks onions are sold in.

clue.text: Drink not right for social gathering

indicators.note: R, the abbreviation for right, is taken away

parts.note: beer is a drink

explanation.surface: Drinking isn't proper at a social event.
explanation.definitionFit: A gathering for communal work or fun, like a sewing or spelling meeting, is called this.

clue.text: My regular visits to Gateshead

indicators.note: taking letters at regular intervals, every third one, from the town name

explanation.surface: I make routine trips to Gateshead.
explanation.walkthrough: Gateshead is a town in north-east England, by Newcastle. 'My' is the exclamation, not the possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild exclamations of surprise, as in 'My, how you've grown'.

clue.text: Actor and singer cast in a chimerical revue

indicators.note: to cast is to throw, sending the letters into a new shape

explanation.surface: A performer is given a role in a fantastical revue.
explanation.walkthrough: Maurice is also a Bee Gee.
explanation.definitionFit: He was a French entertainer who acted in Hollywood films such as Gigi and sang in music halls.

clue.text: Team raving about fan

indicators.note: the word for raving goes about the fan

parts.note: raving means mad
a nut is an enthusiast, as in fitness nut

explanation.surface: A team going wild over a supporter.
explanation.walkthrough: Manchester United is an English football club.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the common short name of Manchester United, a football club.

clue.text: See 16
Unemotional person clings, with space needed

parts.note: the answer read as wordplay gives C (...) and LINGS (..., plural of ling), spelling the clue word once the space is added

explanation.surface: An aloof person clings on, needing room.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: 'with space needed' tells you to split the clue word as C LINGS.
explanation.definitionFit: A cold, aloof person who shows no warmth is idiomatically called this.

clue.text: Small booth with Observer and Time Out

parts.note: a hut is a small booth or shed
an eye is what observes

explanation.surface: A list of newspapers and magazines: a small booth with the Observer and Time Out.
explanation.walkthrough: The Observer is a British Sunday paper and Time Out a London listings magazine, which hides the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking time out to rest describes sleep, which is the informal sense here.

clue.text: Making threefold part for high voices (mostly home key)

indicators.note: the last letter is lost from the word for the high part

parts.note: the treble is the high part in choral music
in means at home
G is a musical key

explanation.surface: A musical arrangement tripled for high voices.
explanation.definitionFit: To treble is to multiply by three, so this present participle means making threefold.

clue.text: Happy, oddly, caught up in extremely northern storm

indicators.note: the letters are caught, held, inside
signals placement inside the word for extremely

parts.note: too means extremely

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read bottom to top
the odd-numbered letters of Happy are used

explanation.surface: A cheerful person gets trapped in a fierce northern storm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Happy' looks like a mood in the scene, but only its odd letters are used; 'up' reverses them because this is a down clue, and 'extremely' gives the word for too much.
explanation.definitionFit: A violent tropical cyclone in the western Pacific is this kind of storm.

clue.text: Fool clenches fist, knocking out posh Aussie

indicators.note: the fool holds the shortened fist inside

parts.note: a nelly is a silly person

indicators.note: removes the posh letter from the fist

parts.note: duke is slang for a fist
U means upper class

explanation.surface: A fool clenches a fist and knocks out a posh Australian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocking out' looks like a boxing blow; it removes U from DUKE, leaving DKE. A nelly, as in 'not on your nelly', is British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: He was a famous Australian bushranger, an outlaw hanged in 1880.

clue.text: Outlandish point by Times, relating to the Listener

parts.note: E, for east, is a compass point
X is the multiplication sign
otic means relating to the ear, the organ that listens

explanation.surface: An odd point made by the Times about the Listener.
explanation.walkthrough: The Times and the Listener (a crossword series it runs) look like newspapers; here they are the times sign and the ear.
explanation.definitionFit: Something exotic is strikingly foreign or unusual, a synonym for bizarre or alien.

clue.text: Fast food from Bake Off? Nonsense!

indicators.note: something off has gone wrong, so the letters are disordered

parts.note: BS is slang for nonsense

explanation.surface: A snack from the TV baking contest dismissed as rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: Bake Off is a British TV baking competition.
explanation.definitionFit: Skewered grilled meat is a takeaway staple, a classic quick meal.

clue.text: Mechanic agrees: roughly £500

indicators.note: done roughly, the letters are arranged untidily

parts.note: monkey is British slang for five hundred pounds

explanation.surface: A mechanic agrees a price of about five hundred pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roughly' looks like an approximation of the money; it rearranges AGREES.
explanation.definitionFit: This informal phrase means a car mechanic, someone who works with oily engines.

clue.text: See 10
Notably two-in-one record player

indicators.note: the two notes go in the one

parts.note: so is one note of the scale
two musical notes, te and re

explanation.surface: A combined record player, notably two units in one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notably' says the numbers count notes of the sol-fa scale.
explanation.definitionFit: A sound system with two channels is commonly called by this name, so it serves as a record player.

clue.text: Search round for small band

parts.note: to comb is to search thoroughly
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: Looking around for a small group of musicians.
explanation.definitionFit: A small jazz or pop group is informally called by this name.

clue.text: See 16
Architect from 15 14 repeatedly visiting Iceland

parts.note: the answer to 15 is the name of the letter G

indicators.note: visitors go inside, so the letters sit within the code

parts.note: IS is the international code for Iceland

indicators.note: repeatedly means more than once, so the letter from the cross-reference to 14 appears twice in a row

parts.note: the answer to 14 is the name of the letter B

explanation.surface: An architect from the Bee Gees, visiting Iceland again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: James Gibbs designed St Martin-in-the-Fields in London; Gibb is also the Bee Gees' surname.
explanation.definitionFit: James Gibbs was an eighteenth-century British designer of churches and the Radcliffe Camera.

clue.text: Party with sister Ruby, perhaps, back in Australia?

parts.note: a do is a party
a nun is a religious sister

indicators.note: the colour word is read backwards

parts.note: ruby is an example of red

explanation.surface: A party with a sister named Ruby back home in Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruby' looks like the sister's name; it is the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: This phrase is a nickname for Australia and New Zealand, so it means located there.
